# A message queue as an extension

[pgmq](https://github.com/pgmq/pgmq) is a message queue in the style of Amazon SQS, written as a
Postgres extension in plain SQL. A queue is a table, and every operation (`pgmq.send`, `pgmq.read`,
`pgmq.delete`, `pgmq.archive` and the rest) is a SQL function, so any program that can run SQL can
send or receive messages, from psql to a trigger to a Go service. Instead of locking the messages it
hands out, pgmq hides each one for a set number of seconds, after which it becomes visible again.

## Visibility timeout

`read` moves a message's `vt` timestamp into the future, and no other reader sees the message until
that moment passes. A queue's life in SQL looks like this:

```sql
SELECT pgmq.create('jobs');
SELECT pgmq.send('jobs', '{"page": "orm/quickstart"}');
SELECT msg_id, read_ct, message FROM pgmq.read('jobs', 30, 1);   -- hidden for 30 s
SELECT pgmq.archive('jobs', 1);                                  -- done: moved to pgmq.a_jobs
```

A consumer that finishes its work deletes or archives the message.
In the [pgmq notebook](../notebooks/pgmq_playground.ipynb), a message read with a
2 second timeout by a consumer that then died came back 2.2 seconds later with `read_ct` 2.

## Delivery guarantees

Delivery is at least once, so a message can reach more than one consumer. pgmq cannot tell a slow
consumer from a broken one, which is why long work has to call `set_vt` to extend its lease (the
time it keeps the message hidden). In the notebook, a 3 second job on a 2 second timeout lost its
message to a second consumer, and the same job kept it when it extended the lease every half
second. `pop` reads and deletes a message in one statement instead, which gives at-most-once
delivery, and a message that a consumer pops and then fails on is lost.

## Retries

pgmq has no retry policy of its own, but `read_ct` and `set_vt` are enough to build one:

```python
for msg_id, read_ct, message in read_batch():
    try:
        handle(message)
        archive(msg_id)
    except Exception:
        if read_ct >= 3:
            with conn.transaction():       # in exactly one of the two queues, always
                send("jobs_dead", message)
                delete("jobs", msg_id)
        else:
            set_vt(msg_id, 2 ** read_ct)  # backoff
```

The notebook runs this loop against a flaky page and a broken one. The flaky page succeeds on its
second attempt, and the broken one moves to the dead-letter queue after its third.

## Consumers and notifications

`read` claims messages with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` inside one `UPDATE`, so many consumers can read
the same queue without overlap. In the notebook, four threads reading 400 messages took exactly 100
each, none twice, in 0.12 s. A consumer can wait for messages inside Postgres with
`read_with_poll`, or `enable_notify_insert` can add a trigger that sends `NOTIFY` on
`pgmq.q_<name>.INSERT`. From send to receipt, a notification took about 12 ms (median of 8), while
polling took up to its interval.

pgmq also supports:

- delayed messages, where `send(queue, msg, delay)` sets `vt` in the future at insert time
- FIFO groups, where messages with the same `x-pgmq-group` header come out of `read_grouped` in
  order, one at a time (a plain `read` ignores groups, so every consumer of the queue has to use the
  grouped functions)
- topics, where `bind_topic('orders.*.paid', 'payments')` and `send_topic('orders.eu.paid', msg)`
  route messages with RabbitMQ-style wildcards, `*` matching one word and `#` any number of words
  after a dot
- archive tables, `pgmq.a_<name>`, which keep every archived message with its `archived_at` time

## pgmq and pgqueuer compared

Both pgmq and [pgqueuer](pgqueuer.qmd) claim work with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, and neither holds a
lock while the work runs. They differ in how a claim expires and in where the logic lives. In pgmq
the claim is a timestamp that the consumer keeps pushing forward, while in pgqueuer it is a `picked`
status whose heartbeat the library refreshes.

| | pgmq | pgqueuer |
|---|---|---|
| what it is | a Postgres extension, SQL functions | a Python library over plain tables |
| a claim | `read` pushes `vt` ahead | dequeue sets `status = 'picked'` |
| a claim expires | when `vt` passes, unless the consumer calls `set_vt` | when the worker's heartbeat is older than `heartbeat_timeout`, refreshed for you |
| consumers | any language with a Postgres driver | Python asyncio workers |
| waking up | `read_with_poll`, or `enable_notify_insert` and `LISTEN` | `LISTEN ch_pgqueuer`, always on |
| retries | by hand, from `read_ct` and `set_vt` | built in, with `on_failure="hold"` |
| extras | archive, topics, FIFO groups, partitioned queues | dedupe keys, fleet-wide limits, cron schedules |

pgmq suits a queue that several languages or services share, or one fed from SQL itself, where an
SQS-like API matters. pgqueuer suits a Python application that wants a worker framework with
retries, limits and schedules already written.
